def: Coating of a microbe or cell with antibodies or complement (opsonins) so phagocytes can recognize and engulf it. Opsonized platelets or red cells are destroyed in the spleen.
A liver-made inhibitor of plasmin that stops fibrinolysis. Its deficiency causes bleeding from excess clot breakdown.
An uncoupling agent that carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the gradient so heat is made instead of ATP. Causes hyperthermia.
Activity of the glycogen debranching enzyme that moves three glucose units from a branch to the end of another chain. Deficiency causes Cori disease.
The branched glycogen remnant left after phosphorylase has trimmed chains to four glucose units from a branch. It accumulates in Cori disease from debranching enzyme deficiency.
Caused by cholesterol crystal emboli breaking off an atherosclerotic plaque, occluding small vessels downstream. Seen after catheterization and in the kidneys, skin (blue toes) and eyes.
Relating to the adenoids and tonsils. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the leading cause of obstructive sleep apnea in children.
A class of drugs including theophylline and caffeine that inhibit phosphodiesterase and block adenosine receptors, relaxing airway smooth muscle.
A monoclonal antibody against the IL-5 receptor alpha used for severe eosinophilic asthma.
A monoclonal antibody against IL-5 used for severe eosinophilic asthma and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
An IL-5 neutralizing monoclonal antibody for severe eosinophilic asthma, given intravenously.
Destruction of ubiquitin-tagged or misfolded proteins by the proteasome. In the common CFTR delta-F508 mutation, misfolded CFTR is degraded before reaching the cell surface.
Thickened and dried out, as in inspissated mucus in cystic fibrosis or inspissated meconium causing meconium ileus.
Kidney arteries running between the renal pyramids, branches of segmental arteries that lead to the arcuate arteries.
A small body fluid compartment of fluid secreted by epithelial cells, such as cerebrospinal, synovial, pleural and intraocular fluids.
The proximal tubule's tendency to reabsorb a fixed fraction of the filtered load, so reabsorption rises as GFR rises.
A toxic metabolite of ethylene glycol made by alcohol dehydrogenase, causing anion gap metabolic acidosis. Further metabolized to oxalate.
Structural or functional blockage to urine flow, such as from stones, posterior urethral valves or prostate enlargement, causing hydronephrosis and kidney injury.
The protein encoded by PKD1 and PKD2, which forms calcium-permeable channels in renal cilia. Mutations cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Deposition of homogeneous, glassy pink protein material in tissue, such as in the glomerular capillaries and arterioles of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
The point where the ureter enters the bladder, one of three narrow sites where kidney stones lodge.
Overgrowth of one side of the body or part of it, as in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Raises risk of Wilms tumor.
Also pyroglutamic acid, an organic acid that accumulates in chronic acetaminophen use and causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Intravenous feeding (total parenteral nutrition) that provides calories and nutrients; can cause hyperchloremic acidosis if chloride-rich solutions are used.
Also globotriaosylceramide, the glycolipid that accumulates in Fabry disease because alpha-galactosidase A is deficient.
A mucopolysaccharidosis from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, causing coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly and intellectual disability.
Phenylalanine breakdown products, including phenylpyruvate and phenyllactate, that spill into urine in phenylketonuria, giving a musty odor.
A phenylalanine byproduct that builds up and is excreted in urine in phenylketonuria.
The keto acid formed from phenylalanine by transamination when phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient, as in phenylketonuria.
An intermediate in tyrosine breakdown formed from homogentisic acid by homogentisate oxidase. The enzyme is deficient in alkaptonuria.
The product left after S-adenosylmethionine donates a methyl group; it is hydrolyzed to homocysteine.
An enzyme that transfers a methyl group, usually from S-adenosylmethionine. PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine, and DNA methyltransferases silence genes.
A DNA building block nucleoside. In adenosine deaminase deficiency it accumulates as dATP, which is toxic to lymphocytes and causes SCID.
The active form of vitamin B12 that is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.
Around hair follicles. Perifollicular hemorrhages and corkscrew hairs are characteristic of scurvy.
The linear tetrapyrrole made from porphobilinogen by porphobilinogen deaminase, deficient in acute intermittent porphyria.
A heme synthesis intermediate; coproporphyrinogen III is formed from uroporphyrinogen III and converted to protoporphyrinogen IX by coproporphyrinogen oxidase.
An alpha-2 agonist muscle relaxant used for spasticity, reducing motor neuron excitation. Causes sedation, hypotension and hepatotoxicity.
A sickle cell test in which sodium metabisulfite, a reducing agent, deoxygenates red cells so HbS-containing cells sickle. Cannot separate trait from disease.
Promoting blood clot formation, such as in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria or antiphospholipid syndrome.
Having fewer cells than normal, as in the marrow of aplastic anemia where fat replaces blood-forming cells.
Increased basophils in the blood. Uncommon; can signal myeloproliferative neoplasms such as chronic myeloid leukemia.
Specialized muscle fibers inside muscle spindles that sense stretch. They are innervated by gamma motor neurons.
Ordinary contractile skeletal muscle fibers outside spindles, innervated by alpha motor neurons.
Onasemnogene abeparvovec, a gene therapy delivering a working SMN1 gene by AAV9 vector for spinal muscular atrophy.
Describes a blood smear with immature white cells and nucleated red cells, suggesting bone marrow infiltration or fibrosis.
Elevated monocyte count in the blood, seen in chronic infections (TB, endocarditis), inflammation and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia.
Inward rotation of the top of the eye toward the nose, a function of the superior oblique and superior rectus muscles. Trochlear nerve palsy impairs it.
Describes nuclei that appear brain-like, with deep folds. Seen in Sezary cells of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
Relating to the labyrinth, the inner ear's vestibular and cochlear structures. Labyrinthitis causes vertigo and hearing loss.
A descending tract from the brainstem reticular formation that helps control posture and locomotion by modulating spinal motor neurons.
Inability to perform rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hand, a sign of cerebellar disease.
The suspensory ligaments that connect the ciliary body to the lens. They tighten to flatten the lens for distance vision.
Relating to the episclera, the thin vascular tissue over the sclera. Episcleral veins receive aqueous humor outflow, and episcleritis causes mild redness.
Intense itching triggered by contact with water, with no rash, classically in polycythemia vera.
Relating to the paracortex of a lymph node, the T cell zone between follicles and the medulla. Enlarges in viral infections and with phenytoin.
Macrophages in germinal centers that contain debris of apoptotic B cells. Their presence supports a reactive rather than neoplastic follicle.
Derivation of all cells in a population from a single clone, a feature of cancer, in contrast to the polyclonal pattern of reactive proliferation.
Describes lymphoid cells whose nuclei lack indentations. Noncleaved cells (centroblasts) are counted to grade follicular lymphoma.
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, linked to chronic inflammation such as H. pylori gastritis and Sjogren syndrome.
Unawareness of one side of space, typically the left, after a right parietal lobe lesion such as a middle cerebral artery stroke.
